On Monday, January 14, 2013 5:41:56 AM UTC-8, mathlover wrote:

I tried running the mapreduce & RHadoop logistic regression test using a different data set with the rmr2 package and comparing the result with logistic regression using glm().  The results don’t match even remotely.  Your thoughts would be greatly appreciated.

The original test code can be found at https://github.com/RevolutionAnalytics/RHadoop/blob/master/rmr2/pkg/tests/logistic-regression.R .

My test code which requires the installation of the R package catdata is as follows:

library(rmr2)
library(catdata)

logistic.regression = 
  function(input, iterations, dims, alpha){
      lr.map =          
      function(., M) {
        Y = M[,1]
        X = M[,-1]
        keyval(
          1,
          Y * X * 
            g(-Y * as.numeric(X %*% t(plane))))
      }

      lr.reduce =
      function(k, Z) 
        keyval(k, t(as.matrix(apply(Z,2,sum))))

      plane = t(rep(0, dims))
      g = function(z) 1/(1 + exp(-z))
      for (i in 1:iterations) {
            gradient = 
            values(
            from.dfs(
                  mapreduce(
                  input,
                  map = lr.map,
                  reduce = lr.reduce,
                  combine = T)))
            plane = plane + alpha * gradient
      }
     plane 
}

data(foodstamp)
testdata = to.dfs(as.matrix(foodstamp))
print(logistic.regression(testdata, 10, 3, 0.05))
print(coef(glm(y ~ TEN + SUP + INC, data=foodstamp, family=binomial)))

Output from the run:

      TEN SUP   INC
[1,] 0.15 0.3 222.2

(Intercept)          TEN          SUP          INC
-0.340026643 -1.760299816  0.775245518 -0.001489027

parts:
My reference is this paper:http://qwone.com/~jason/writing/lr.pdf
In that paper the response is encoded as +-1 and the need for an intercept is eliminated by using a dummy independent variable. Of course your data doesn't have a dummy variable and the encoding is 0,1. Correcting that doesn't make the answer the same as glm though, so something else is going on.


Antonio

The paper does call for a bias term that is set 0 and it needs a corresponding weight.  

So, I think we need to write the test code as follows:

testdata.df = data.frame(y = 2 * (eps > 0) - 1, x0 = 1, x1 = 1:test.size, x2 = 1:test.size + eps)
testdata = to.dfs(as.matrix(testdata.df))

Also, we would need to fix up the definition of plane to account for the additional weight:
plane = t(c(1, rep(0, dims)))

However, the dataset I used, I am not sure how to reconcile the fact that glm() calls for y to be 0 or 1 while the mapreduce example calls for y to be -1 or 1.

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#499] Re: Logistic Regression using rmr2 package
parts:
The test code appears to work.  I wrote the test case below without mapreduce.  My guess is that since glm() uses Y values of 0/1, we shouldn't expect the coefficients of the fitted model to match the coefficients of the test model which uses Y values of -1/1.  The gradient descent method used by the test code converges very slowly which is why I used a large number of iterations.

dims = 2
alpha = 0.05
test.size = 5

eps = rnorm(test.size)
# x0 is bias column
testdata.df = data.frame(y = 2 * (eps > 0) - 1, x0 = 1, x1 = 1:test.size, x2 = 1:test.size + eps)
M = as.matrix(testdata.df)

Y = M[,1]
X = M[,-1]
plane = t(c(1, rep(0, dims)))
g = function(z) 1/(1 + exp(-z))

for (i in 1:1000000) {
    plane = plane + alpha * t(as.matrix(apply(Y * X * g(-Y * as.numeric(X %*% t(plane))), 2, sum))) }

cat("plane:\n")
print(plane)
cat("M:\n")
print(M)
cat("\n")

# Check results
for (i in 1:test.size) {
    # Calculate conditional probability
    p = g(apply(X[i,] %*% t(plane), 2, sum))
    cat("Y[", i, "]=", Y[i], " p(Y=1|X)=", p, " ",
        ifelse(Y[i] == 1,
            ifelse(abs(1 - p) < 0.01, "passed", "failed"),
   ifelse(p < 0.01, "passed", "failed")),
"\n", sep='')
}

This has helped   in preserving the equivalence of the two backends and also the correctness of each (because the two backends tend to have different bugs)

library(rmr2)

logistic.regression = 
  function(input, iterations, dims, alpha){
      lr.map =

        keyval(

      }
     plane 
}

be stands for backend. So the same code is executed twice on two different backends. That they are identical is part of the assertions that the package has to satisfy to be ready for release. This has helped   in preserving the equivalence of the two backends and also the correctness of each (because the two backends tend to have different bugs)


Antonio
